raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.
raw_language.Name: Tocharian A
raw_language.Variety: Tocharian A, the relatively uniform language attested in texts of almost exclusively religious content, from Šorčuq and Turfan.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set at a point geographically roughly intermediate between the two main areas where Tocharian A texts have been found: Šorčuq and Turfan.

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.
raw_language.Name: Tocharian A
raw_language.Variety: Tocharian A, the relatively uniform language attested in texts of almost exclusively religious content, from Šorčuq and Turfan.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set at a point geographically roughly intermediate between the two main areas where Tocharian A texts have been found: Šorčuq and Turfan.

raw_cognateset.Justification: Anatolian, Tocharian, Hellenic, Armenian, Albanian, Indo-Iranic, Balto-Slavic, Germanic, Italic, and Celtic lexemes reflecting the Indo-European inherited word for 'name' (cf. [EIEC](src-657) 390-391). Certain details of the reconstruction of the PIE word are disputed (cf. [Stüber 1998](src-315):53-59), but a general shape *Hneh₃-mn̥ with different ablaut variants of the root and suffix tend to be agreed upon. Debate on the identity of the initial laryngeal as *h₁ or *h₃ hinge on interpretation of the Doric Greek forms in ἐνυμα- versus the ὄνομα forms more commonly found elsewhere (cf. esp. discussions of [EWAia](src-172) II:35-37, [Beekes 2010](src-66):1084-1085). Cf. also [Kloekhorst 2008](src-80):517-519, [Adams 2013](src-345):288, [Martirosyan 2010](src-79):96-97, [Demiraj 1997](src-369):165, [Orel 1998](src-105):87, [Derksen 2015](src-353):556-557, [Derksen 2008](src-81):212, [Kroonen 2013](src-165):382-383, [de Vaan 2008](src-54):412-413, [Matasović 2009](src-50):38).

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.

raw_language.Variety: Tocharian A, the relatively uniform language attested in texts of almost exclusively religious content, from Šorčuq and Turfan.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set at a point geographically roughly intermediate between the two main areas where Tocharian A texts have been found: Šorčuq and Turfan.

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.

raw_language.Variety: Tocharian A, the relatively uniform language attested in texts of almost exclusively religious content, from Šorčuq and Turfan.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set at a point geographically roughly intermediate between the two main areas where Tocharian A texts have been found: Šorčuq and Turfan.

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.

raw_language.Variety: Tocharian A, the relatively uniform language attested in texts of almost exclusively religious content, from Šorčuq and Turfan.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set at a point geographically roughly intermediate between the two main areas where Tocharian A texts have been found: Šorčuq and Turfan.

raw_cognateset.Justification: Two variants *kʷr̥mi- and *u̯r̥mi- in the same meaning 'worm' are generally reconstructed for PIE. The variant *u̯r̥mi- attested in Germanic and Italic might have been secondary from *kʷr̥mi- (cf. {de Vaan 2008}:665), but it may also be possible that the two lexemes were a rhyming pair already in Indo-European poetic language (cf. [Watkins 1987](src-696):288). Cf. also [Demiraj 1997](src-369):225-226, [Orel 1998](src-105):197, [EWAia](src-172) I:394-395, [ALEW](src-352) 493-494, [Derksen 2015](src-353):246, [ESSJa](src-458) 4:171-172 [Derksen 2008](src-81)93-94, [Matasović 2009](src-50):181-182.

Manichaean Sogd. kyrm- 'Schlange', MPers. klm (kirm) 'Wurm, Drache, Schlange', NPers. kirm 'Wurm, Schlange'), from PIE *kʷr̥mi- (cf. OIr. cruim, W., Bret. pryf 'Wurm', Lith. kirmìs 'Wurm, Schlange', Sloven. čr̂m 'Fingerwurm, Karbunkel', etc.). Beside *kʷr̥mi- exists "a rhyme formation in Indo-European probably for reason of tabu" *u̯r̥mi- (NHG Wurm, cf. Lat. vermis), (so Watkins 1987:288).}];696[288{"[T]he word for 'worm, serpent, dragon' [in Germanic] is Old English wyrm, Old Norse ormr, Old Saxon and Old High German wurm, Gothic waurms: Germanic *wurmiz exactly cognate with Latin vermis, and presupposing Indo-European *u̯r̥mis. The word is a rhyme formation in Indo-European to *kʷr̥mis, probably for reason of tabu| kʷr̥mis is found in Celtic, Balto-Slavic, Albanian and Indo-Iranian. The usual meaning of *kʷr̥mis is just 'worm' in most traditions, but in Middle Iranian it is also the word for 'dragon'| compare the Pahlavi version of the familiar Indo-European formula: kirm ōzat 'slew the dragon' (Kārnāmak IX). There can be no doubt that in *u̯r̥mis/*kʷr̥mis we have two variants of the same designation of the Indo-European mythological serpent-adversary."}];353[246{S.v. raw_cognateset.Justification: Germanic and Italic lexemes as though from PIE *kólso- 'neck' (cf. [Ringe 2006](src-395):95, [Kroonen 2013](src-165):205, [EWA 4](src-415) 777-780, [de Vaan 2008](src-54):125). Root etymology disputed. Root reference form for this set follows the reconstruction of [Ringe 2006](src-395):95. If ultimately from PIE *kʷelh₁- 'to turn' ([LIV²](src-141) 386-388), then these lexemes may be root-cognate with the Baltic lexemes in [cognate set 1868](cog-1868), but the etymology of the Baltic lexemes is less than certain; cf. further discussion in that cognate class. Alternatively a root etymology has been proposed to PIE *kelH- 'to tower, soar' (cf. [EWA 4](src-415) 477-480).

The Brythonic lexemes in this class are sometimes considered to be (parallel?) loanwords from Latin (cf. [Matasović 2009](src-50):293-294, [Deshayes 2003](src-309):539-540), but by others to be inherited (cf. [Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru (GPC)](src-236), [Falileyev 2000](src-240):121, [NIL](src-274) 509n10). The assumption that these lexemes are inherited has been followed here.

raw_cognateset.Justification: Tocharian, Hellenic, Armenian, Balto-Slavic, Germanic, Italic, and Celtic lexemes derived from PIE *sal- 'salt' ([NIL](src-274) 586-590, [EIEC](src-657) 498, [IEW](src-49) 878-879, cf. [Adams 2013](src-345):742, [Beekes 2010](src-66):177, [Martirosyan 2010](src-79):24, 40-41, [ALEW](src-352) 887-888, [Derksen 2015](src-353):548-549, [Derksen 2008](src-81):461, [Kroonen 2013](src-165):425, [de Vaan 2008](src-54):535, [Matasović 2009](src-50):319). The root is difficult to reconstruct; the traditional reconstruction as *sal- has been followed here after [NIL](src-274), but note in order to avoid reconstructing PIE *a the Leiden school reconstructs a hysterokinetic l-stem: nom.sg. *séh₂‑l‑s, acc.sg. *sh₂‑el‑m, gen.sg. *sh₂‑l‑ós ([Kortlandt 1985b](src-640):119, [Beekes 1995](src-72):177, cf. also [Rieken 1999](src-317):424n2103). The Germanic forms in this set show an extension in *d which may be on analogy to *su̯eh₂d- 'sweet' [cognate set 5109](cog-5109), alternatively the *-d- might be explained as a compound with the root *deh₃- 'give' (cf. [ALEW](src-352) 886-887 s.v. Old Lithuanian saldùs 'sweet' and further discussion in [cognate set 5157](cog-5157)).

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.
raw_language.Name: Tocharian A
raw_language.Variety: Tocharian A, the relatively uniform language attested in texts of almost exclusively religious content, from Šorčuq and Turfan.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set at a point geographically roughly intermediate between the two main areas where Tocharian A texts have been found: Šorčuq and Turfan.

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.

raw_cognateset.Justification: Tocharian, Armenian, Indo-Iranic, Balto-Slavic, Germanic, Italic, and Celtic lexemes derived from PIE *dn̥g̑ʰu̯éh₂- 'tongue'. The forms as attested appear to have undergone multiple contaminations in several daughter languages: (1) The Tocharian forms reflect *ĝn̥dʰu̯éh₂- ← PIE *dn̥g̑ʰu̯éh₂- by metathesis of place of articulation (cf. [Ringe 1996](src-695):45-6, [Hilmarsson 1996](src-149):79, [Adams 2013](src-345):147). (2) Balto-Slavic lexemes appear to have lost initial *d- already at a common Balto-Slavic stage ([Derksen 2008](src-81):159, [Derksen 2015](src-353):285, cf. [ESSJa](src-458) 6:74-75). (3) Armenian, Italic, and Lithuanian lexemes appear to have independently contaminated with initial l-, probably under influence of their respective regular reflexes of PIE *lei̯g̑ʰ- 'to lick' ([Martirosyan 2010](src-79):307-308, [de Vaan 2008](src-54):343, {ref Derksen 2015:285). (4) Celtic forms appear to have undergone a distance assimilation *dengʷāt- > *tengʷāt-  ([Matasović 2009](src-50):368). (5) Indo-Iranic forms have a similar preform *ºg̑ʰu̯eh₂-/*ºg̑ʰuh₂- to the form *dn̥g̑ʰu̯eh₂- found in other branches, but instead appears to i-reduplicate the initial syllable (cf. notes to Ved. jihvā́- in [EWAia](src-172) I:591-593). Additionally, the Iranian forms appear to show a different Anlaut from the Indic ones (Indic *j-, Iranian *s-). This small deviation aside, the Indo-Iranic forms appear to go back to basic form *ji-ju̯aH-/*ji-juH- (vel sim.) in Proto-Indo-Iranic. This apparent reduplication could be secondary reanalysis of an original *dn̥g̑ʰu̯eh₂-/*dn̥g̑ʰuh₂- > *daju̯aH-/dajuH- as a reduplicated form *ji-ju̯aH-, (cf. forms such as *kʷe-kʷl-o- > cakra- 'wheel'), cf. [Mallory & Adams 2006](src-75):175. For the purposes of root-cognacy, The Indo-Iranic forms are treated in this class as cognate with the other forms which are more clearly from PIE *dn̥g̑ʰ-u̯eh₂-/*dn̥g̑ʰ-uh₂-. The least disturbed forms appear to be found in Germanic, for which see [Lehmann 1986](src-179):349, [Kroonen 2013](src-165):526-527.

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.

raw_language.Variety: Tocharian A, the relatively uniform language attested in texts of almost exclusively religious content, from Šorčuq and Turfan.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set at a point geographically roughly intermediate between the two main areas where Tocharian A texts have been found: Šorčuq and Turfan.

raw_cognateset.Justification: Hellenic, Armenian, Indo-Iranic, Baltic, Germanic, Italic, and Celtic lexemes continuing an inherited word for 'tooth', widely considered to continue a participle *h₁d-ónt- to the verbal root *h₁ed- *'to bite' → 'to eat', lexicalised as 'tooth' already in PIE ([NIL](src-274) 208-220, [LIV²](src-141) 230-231, [EIEC](src-657) 594). Under this explanation the original Ancient Greek form would be continued by Aeolic ἔδοντ-, which underwent vowel assimilation in other dialects. The Leiden School of Indo-European reconstruction alternatively reconstructs a distinct root *h₃ed- 'to bite, sting' following [Kortlandt 2003](src-549):77, who argues that it would better account for ὀδών much more straightforwardly, and it would also much better account for the Ancient Greek privative adjective νωδός 'toothless' < *n̥-h₃d-ó-, (expected †νηδός < *n̥-h₃d-ó-); as for Aeolic ἔδοντ-, it only occurs in late grammatical texts and could have itself been created on the basis of an analogy to Greek ἔδ- 'eat'. For individual branches, cf. [Chantraine 1968–1980](src-270):776, [Beekes 2010](src-66):1049, [Martirosyan 2010](src-79):1049, [EWAia](src-172) I:693-694, [ALEW](src-352) 174-175, [Derksen 2015](src-353):115, [Ernout & Meillet 1985](src-316):169, [de Vaan 2008](src-54):166-167, [Vendryes et al. 1959–1996](src-296) D:62-63 [Matasović 2009](src-50):90).

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).

raw_language.Variety: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region.

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. raw_cognateset.Justification: Anatolian, Hellenic, Armenian, Albanian, Indo-Iranic, Italic, and Celtic lexemes continuing PIE *h₂ost-, the inherited Indo-European word for 'bone' ([EIEC](src-657) 77, cf. [Kloekhorst 2008](src-80):325-326, [Adams 2013](src-345):48-50, [Beekes 2010](src-66):1119, [Martirosyan 2010](src-79):533, [Demiraj 1997](src-369):82-83, [Orel 1998](src-105):11, [EWAia](src-172) I:150-151, [ESIJa](src-331) 1:232-234, [de Vaan 2008](src-54):436-437, [Matasović 2009](src-50):44-45). Perhaps cognate with the lexemes from Proto-Slavic *kost- with [cognate set 1114](cog-1114) but the explanation of the initial k- is unclear (cf. further discussion in that cognate set). The PIE stem is usually reconstructed with initial *h₂- on the basis of Greek ἀστραγαλός 'knucklebone' (cf. [Chantraine 1968–1980](src-270):129), but the etymological connection of this word to the lexemes in this class is rejected by [Beekes 2010](src-66):157-158 who prefers to see Greek ἀστραγαλός as a substratum loanword.

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).

raw_language.Variety: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set on Kuča, since manuscript evidence indicates that the original location of Tocharian B speakers was Kuča and its environs (including Qumtura and Subashi) — see especially Peyrot (2008).

For the purposes of providing a root reference form for this cognate set, we have followed the analysis of [Beekes 2004](src-702), cf. also [Beekes 2010](src-66):470-471) s.v. Ancient Greek ἕσπερος. Exceptionally against the these lexemes forming a class, cf. [LIPP 2](src-294) s.v. †*u̯é-kʷsp-ero-. Cf. also [Derksen 2008](src-81):513, [ALEW](src-352) 1174-1175, [Martirosyan 2010](src-79):215-216. If *k⁽ʷ⁾sep- is the lexical root underlying this formation, then these lexemes may ultimately be cognate with Hittite išpant-, Vedic kṣáp- 'night', etc. in [cognate set 87](cog-87).

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).
raw_language.Name: Tocharian B
raw_language.Variety: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set on Kuča, since manuscript evidence indicates that the original location of Tocharian B speakers was Kuča and its environs (including Qumtura and Subashi) — see especially Peyrot (2008).

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).

raw_language.Variety: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set on Kuča, since manuscript evidence indicates that the original location of Tocharian B speakers was Kuča and its environs (including Qumtura and Subashi) — see especially Peyrot (2008).

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).

raw_language.Description: Magahi is spoken mainly in Bihar and Jharkhand, along with parts of West Bengal and Orissa. The IE-CoR data were collected from the variety of Magahi spoken in and around the capital city of Patna, Jehanabad and Gaya.  Although Magahi is linguistically different from Hindi (it does not even belong to same sub-branch, in Grierson's classification), the Indian government classifies Magahi as a dialect of Hindi.  Nonetheless, a large population (up to 13,978,565 according to the Census of India, 2001) residing in villages and small towns still speak and identify Magahi as their medium of communication (Alok et al 2011).

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).
raw_language.Name: Tocharian B
raw_language.Variety: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set on Kuča, since manuscript evidence indicates that the original location of Tocharian B speakers was Kuča and its environs (including Qumtura and Subashi) — see especially Peyrot (2008).

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).
raw_language.Name: Tocharian B
raw_language.Variety: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set on Kuča, since manuscript evidence indicates that the original location of Tocharian B speakers was Kuča and its environs (including Qumtura and Subashi) — see especially Peyrot (2008).

Since [Watkins 1973](src-711) the Celtic words have been connected to Hittite and Palaic words for 'river' from a PIE n-stem *h₂ebʰ-n-, more recently followed by [Willi 2004](src-710) and [Kloekhorst 2008](src-80):294-295 s.v. Hitt. ḫapa-. A popular alternative analysis reconciles the Celtic words with Indo-Iranic words for 'water' (cf. [cognate set 157](cog-157)) and Baltic and Nuristani lexemes for 'river' (cf. [cognate set 7856](cog-7856)) via a derivation using the 'Hoffmann Suffix' *h₂ep-h₃on- (cf. [Matasović 2009](src-50):23-24 s.v. raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).

raw_language.Variety: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region.

uncertainty.source_comment: Used both for the internal and external part of body (e.g. it is attested in a phrase 'flat belly'). An alternative lexeme, 'tėsin', was probably used only for the internal part of body (it is strongly suggested by its cognates in other Slavic languages).

raw_cognateset.Justification: Anatolian, Tocharian, Hellenic, Armenian, Indo-Iranic, Balto-Slavic, Germanic, Italic, and Celtic lexemes derived from PIE *h₃neg⁽ʷ⁾ʰ- '(finger)nail' ([Kloekhorst 2008](src-80):723-725, [Beekes 2010](src-66):1086-1087, [Martirosyan 2010](src-79):254-255, [EWAia](src-172) II:4-5, [ALEW](src-352) 681-682, [Derksen 2015](src-353):327, [ESSJa](src-458) 25:161-164, 170-173, [Derksen 2008](src-81):355, [de Vaan 2008](src-54):641, [Matasović 2009](src-50):36). Indo-Iranic forms go back to an aberrant *(H)nákha-; Indo-Aryan forms go back to nakhá- ~ *nakkha-; some show early nasalization due to blend with aṅgúri- ~  aṅgúli- 'finger, toe' (°-aṅgulá-) or aṅguṣṭhá- 'thumb'; aṅká- 'hook' (RV) and later aṅkurá- 'hooked' may also have played a role, cf. [Turner 1962–1966](src-442), no. 6914 + 134f. 137f., 100, 109; Addenda 6914

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.
raw_language.Name: Tocharian A
raw_language.Variety: Tocharian A, the relatively uniform language attested in texts of almost exclusively religious content, from Šorčuq and Turfan.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set at a point geographically roughly intermediate between the two main areas where Tocharian A texts have been found: Šorčuq and Turfan.

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).
raw_language.Name: Tocharian B
raw_language.Variety: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set on Kuča, since manuscript evidence indicates that the original location of Tocharian B speakers was Kuča and its environs (including Qumtura and Subashi) — see especially Peyrot (2008).

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).

Pace [Kroonen 2013](src-165), the different morphology of the Germanic-Italic lexemes on one hand and the Indo-Iranian, and Baltic lexemes on the other does not favour the view that PIE *h₂ekʷ- and *h₂ep- were variants of one another (Martin Kümmel, p.c.). Likewise it is not clear whether the Germanic and Italic lexemes are independent borrowings from a third source (as advocated by [Beekes 1998](src-709)), but in view of the regular correspondences between Italic and Germanic, gratuitous. Further proposed connections are less certain (cf. [EWA 1](src-383) 99-103 for a thorough discussion). Less certain is the connection of the Celtic and Anatolian lexemes (cf. discussion in [cognate set 1735](cog-1735)).

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).

raw_language.Description: Tocharian A texts come from the Šorčuq and Turfan areas and date to not before 7th c. CE. There is continuing debate as to whether the language was still spoken at that time, but there is no evidence that Tocharian A speakers ever lived to the west of Šorčuq. The Turfan texts exhibit a few minor linguistic peculiarities, suggesting that there were once actual living Tocharian A speech communities in both places.

raw_language.Description: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region, attested in manuscripts from the 5th and 6th centuries CE.  From Kuča, the language spread to Šorčuq c. 600 CE, and then eastwards to Turfan and (marginally) westwards to Murtuq in the late 7th century CE.  The archaic/early form of Tocharian B, as targeted in the IE-CoR data, is from Kuča, while what is sometimes termed “classical” Tocharian B, as represented by the majority of the surviving literary manuscripts, comes from Kuča and sites immediately to its east (Šorčuq, Qarašahr, etc.).
raw_language.Name: Tocharian B
raw_language.Variety: Archaic/early Tocharian B of the Kuča region.
raw_language.loc_justification: Set on Kuča, since manuscript evidence indicates that the original location of Tocharian B speakers was Kuča and its environs (including Qumtura and Subashi) — see especially Peyrot (2008).
